raw_case_text:
We report the course of a 51-years-old CMV IgG positive male recipient. He received his fifth kidney transplant from a CMV IgG positive deceased donor in January 2018. As he was highly immunized, the immunosuppressive drug regimen included ATG induction (Thymoglobuline , Genzyme, 1.5mg/kg body weight on day 0, 2, 3, and 4 post transplantation), tacrolimus (Prograf , Astellas, target level 6-8 ng/ml), mycophenolic acid (Myfortic , Novartis, 720 mg b.i.d.) and prednisolone. Valganciclovir (Valcyte , Roche) prophylaxis was given orally for 3 months. During the previous post-transplant periods, the patient had never developed any CMV-related complications. One week after stopping prophylaxis, asymptomatic CMV replication was detected at a level of 57,200 IU/ml (week 14,  Figure 1A ). Kidney function was stable with an eGFR CKD EPI of 63.2 ml/min/1.73 m2, and laboratory parameters were within normal range.
Valganciclovir was initiated again at a therapeutic dosage adapted to renal function (Cockcroft-Gault formula). Despite antiviral therapy, viral load further increased. The patient was admitted to hospital, and antiviral treatment was changed from valganciclovir to i.v. ganciclovir (Cymeven , Roche) from post transplant week 21 until week 23. By the time of admission, the patient had developed leukopenia (week 21), followed by thrombopenia (week 22), and malaise. He therefore received CMV-specific i.v. immunoglobulins (CMV-IVIG, Cytotect CP , Biotest, 5.000 units per week, from week 21), and mycophenolate sodium was stopped and replaced by everolimus in week 22 (Certican , Novartis, target level 3-5 ng/ml, mean trough level 4.69 ng/ml). As CMV viral load still increased, resistance testing was initiated (Institute of Virology, Ulm University Medical Center, Germany). The patient developed fever of up to 38.8 C and received antibiotic therapy with piperacillin-tazobactam (Tazobac , Pfizer), although CRP levels never exceeded 2.5 mg/dl. Neither CT thorax scanning nor urine-testing nor blood cultures showed signs of infections. The patient developed diarrhea for three days. Clostridium difficile testing was negative and diarrhea ended spontaneously. In week 23, results from resistance testing returned and revealed the UL54 DNA polymerase gene mutation A834P (without concomitant mutation in the UL97 kinase gene). This mutation confers resistance against ganciclovir, foscarnet, and cidofovir. Although combined treatment with foscarnet and high dose ganciclovir is recommended in this situation, leukopenia and thrombopenia resulted in reluctance to follow this recommendation. As recent studies have shown a favorable effect of cyclosporine A and mTOR inhibitors on BK virus and CMV infection, i.v. ganciclovir was stopped and immunosuppression was switched from tacrolimus to cyclosporine A (Sandimmun , Novartis, target level 80-100 ng/ml) in week 23). In addition, the patient received high dose CMV-specific IVIG for 8 consecutive days (10.000 units per day,  Figure 1A ). Although viral load further increased to 2.813.000 IU/ml during week 24, this regimen resulted in an eventual decrease in CMV load for the first time later in week 24. The patient was discharged from hospital in week 25 with a viral load of 1.386.000 IU/ml, and monitoring was continued in an ambulatory setting. CMV-IVIG treatment was continued with 10.000 units once a week ( Figure 1A ). To analyze the patient s cellular immunocompetence toward CMV, CMV-specific CD4, and CD8 T cells were quantified from whole blood after stimulation using flow-cytometry. In brief, 450 microl of whole blood was stimulated with 32 microl/ml of a CMV lysate (Virion/Serion) and a mixture of 22 CMV-antigen derived MHC class I binding peptides [1 microg/ml, peptide sequences described in ] for a total of 6 h. After 2 h, 10 microg/ml brefeldin A (Sigma) was added to accumulate cytokines intracellularly. A non-infected control lysate (Virion/Serion) served as a negative control. CMV-specific cells were identified as described before after flow-cytometric staining as CD69 positive CD4 and CD8 T cells producing interferon gamma (IFNgamma). Moroever, induction of TNFalpha and IL-2 as well as expression of CTLA-4 was analyzed. A polyclonal stimulation with Staphylococcus aureus Enterotoxin B (SEB) was carried out to assess general immune responsiveness. Interestingly, after discharge from hospital (week 25), CMV-specific CD4 and CD8 T cells were detectable ( Figures 1B, C ). However, consistent with high viral load, absolute counts/microl were very low, and their phenotypical and cytokine expression pattern showed typical signs of functional anergy characterized by high expression of CTLA-4 and limited ability to produce cytokines ( Figure 1B  and data not shown). By week 27, CMV viral load had decreased to 205 IU/ml. This was accompanied by a marked increase in CMV-specific T-cell numbers, which remained at a similarly high level when analyzed in week 33, at which time CMV-IVIG treatment was stopped. In week 34, the patient developed an acute humoral rejection, which was successfully treated with plasmapheresis, high dose corticosteroids and high dose intravenous immunoglobulins. CMV viral load remained low or below detection limit thereafter. One year after transplantation kidney function had stabilized, viral load was undetectable, and CMV-specific T-cell numbers had remained stable. Consistent with successful viral control, CTLA-4 expression and cytokine profile of CMV-specific T cells had normalized over time ( Figures 1B, C ).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 51-year-old CMV-seropositive male fifth-time deceased-donor kidney transplant recipient (CMV D+/R+) developed asymptomatic high-level CMV viremia at post-transplant week 14 (1 week after stopping valganciclovir prophylaxis), progressing by weeks 21-23 to fever (up to 38.8 °C), malaise, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and self-limited diarrhea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Having received his fifth deceased-donor kidney transplant in January 2018 (CMV D+/R+; rabbit ATG induction, tacrolimus, mycophenolic acid, and prednisolone maintenance, plus 3 months of oral valganciclovir prophylaxis), the patient was found at week 14 (1 week after stopping prophylaxis) to have asymptomatic CMV viremia (57,200 IU/mL) with stable graft function (eGFR 63.2 mL/min/1.73m2). Despite therapeutic oral valganciclovir and inpatient switch to intravenous ganciclovir (weeks 21-23), CMV viral load surged to 2,813,000 IU/mL at week 24 accompanied by leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, malaise, fever up to 38.8 °C, and 3 days of diarrhea.
subjective.past_medical_history: End-stage renal disease status post five kidney transplantations (fifth deceased-donor transplant in January 2018; highly sensitized recipient; CMV serostatus D+/R+; no CMV complications during prior four transplants).
subjective.review_of_systems: Initially asymptomatic at week 14; developed malaise, fever up to 38.8 °C, and 3 days of C. difficile-negative diarrhea during weeks 21-23. Medications at week 14: tacrolimus, mycophenolic acid (720 mg BID), and prednisolone.

objective.physical_examination: Fever up to 38.8 °C and general malaise during inpatient admission at weeks 21-23.
objective.routine_investigations: Week 14 baseline eGFR (CKD-EPI) 63.2 mL/min/1.73m2. Week 21-23 labs: leukopenia (week 21), thrombocytopenia (week 22), CRP <=2.5 mg/dL, negative blood and urine cultures, and negative stool Clostridioides difficile testing.
objective.advanced_workup: Thoracic CT showed no pulmonary infection. Quantitative plasma CMV PCR rose from 57,200 IU/mL (week 14) on valganciclovir/IV ganciclovir to a peak of 2,813,000 IU/mL (week 24), then declined following mTOR/cyclosporine conversion and high-dose CMV-IVIG to 1,386,000 IU/mL (week 25 discharge), 205 IU/mL (week 27), and undetectable at 1 year. Genotypic resistance testing at week 23 identified a multidrug-resistant UL54 DNA polymerase mutation A834P (with wild-type UL97 kinase) conferring cross-resistance to ganciclovir, foscarnet, and cidofovir. Whole-blood flow cytometric CMV-specific T-cell monitoring (stimulated with CMV lysate and 22 MHC-I peptides) at week 25 showed low absolute CMV-specific CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell counts with functional anergy (high CTLA-4 expression and blunted IFN-gamma/TNF-alpha/IL-2 production), followed by robust expansion of functional CMV-specific T cells and normalization of CTLA-4 expression from week 27 through 1 year.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of multidrug-resistant cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection caused by a UL54 DNA polymerase A834P mutation (conferring resistance to ganciclovir, foscarnet, and cidofovir; wild-type UL97) in a fifth-time kidney transplant recipient (CMV D+/R+), with peak plasma viral load of 2,813,000 IU/mL. Due to UL54 pan-resistance and myelosuppression (leukopenia/thrombocytopenia), intravenous ganciclovir was stopped, mycophenolic acid was switched to everolimus (week 22, target trough 3-5 ng/mL), tacrolimus was switched to cyclosporine A (week 23, target trough 80-100 ng/ml), and high-dose intravenous CMV-specific hyperimmune globulin (Cytotect CP 10,000 units/day for 8 days then 10,000 units weekly through week 33) was administered. This regimen restored endogenous CMV-specific CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell immunity, reduced CMV load to 205 IU/mL by week 27, and maintained undetectable CMV viremia and stable allograft function at 1 year (despite successful treatment of an intercurrent week 34 acute humoral rejection with plasmapheresis, high-dose steroids, and IVIG).
